verses.text: Follow after love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.
For he who speaks in another language speaks not to men, but to God; for no one understands; but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries.
But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.
He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly.

Now I desire to have you all speak with other languages, but rather that you would prophesy. For he is greater who prophesies than he who speaks with other languages, unless he interprets, that the assembly may be built up.
But now, brothers,  if I come to you speaking with other languages, what would I profit you, unless I speak to you either by way of revelation, or of knowledge, or of prophesying, or of teaching?
Even things without life, giving a voice, whether pipe or harp, if they didn’t give a distinction in the sounds, how would it be known what is piped or harped?
For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war?
So also you, unless you uttered by the tongue words easy to understand, how would it be known what is spoken? For you would be speaking into the air.
There are, it may be, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and none of them is without meaning.
If then I don’t know the meaning of the sound, I would be to him who speaks a foreigner, and he who speaks would be a foreigner to me.
So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound to the building up of the assembly.
Therefore let him who speaks in another language pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in another language, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful.
What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
Otherwise if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the “Amen” at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say?
For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up.
I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all.
However in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language.
Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature.
In the law it is written, “By men of strange languages and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people. Not even thus will they hear me, says the Lord.”
Therefore other languages are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelieving; but prophesying is for a sign, not to the unbelieving, but to those who believe.
If therefore the whole assembly is assembled together and all speak with other languages, and unlearned or unbelieving people come in, won’t they say that you are crazy?
But if all prophesy, and someone unbelieving or unlearned comes in, he is reproved by all, and he is judged by all.
And thus the secrets of his heart are revealed. So he will fall down on his face and worship God, declaring that God is among you indeed.

What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up.
If any man speaks in another language, let it be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself, and to God.
Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others discern.
But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent.
For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be exhorted.
The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets,
for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints.
Let the women be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking except in submission, as the law also says,
if they desire to learn anything. “Let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to be talking in the assembly.”
What!? Was it from you that the word of God went out? Or did it come to you alone?
If any man thinks himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him recognize the things which I write to you, that they are the commandment of the Lord.
But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.
Therefore, brothers, desire earnestly to prophesy, and don’t forbid speaking with other languages.
Let all things be done decently and in order.

footnotes.content: Love is the path, and prophecy—the gift to speak God's truth plainly into a hungry heart—is what Paul urges us to crave. I've noticed how easily we chase what feels impressive instead of what builds others up. He's telling us: chase love first, then ask the Lord for words that heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul doesn't say speaking in a language you don't know is wrong—he says it's just between you and God. Mystery lives there, deep prayer in the Spirit. But notice: nobody else hears what you mean. That's fine for private prayer, but it tells us something about how gifts are meant to land in the assembly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophecy does three things—builds up (edifies), urges onward (exhorts), and soothes a wounded heart (consoles). Three gifts in one voice. When someone speaks God's truth into the room with humility, I've always watched how people's spines straighten, how tears sometimes come. The Lord meets us where we hurt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the hinge: speaking in a language you alone understand edges toward yourself. Prophecy turns outward, toward the gathered people. It's not pride to want to grow strong in prayer—the Spirit prays in us in ways our minds can't follow. But Paul is saying: when we're together, turn your face toward the room. Build the body.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul actually wants everyone to speak in other languages privately—but he'd rather you all prophesy. The gift of interpretation unlocks it for the assembly, and then the whole room is lifted up. It's like saying: pray how you need to pray, but when we gather, let your gift serve the whole family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul turns practical. If he walked into the church speaking in a language only the Spirit understands, what good would that be? He offers the real channels: revelation, knowledge, prophecy, teaching—words the room can hold and be strengthened by. Any gift worth having is worth giving away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An instrument that doesn't make a clear sound—a pipe or harp without distinction—tells you nothing. Paul reaches for the shepherd's world: even objects without life must speak plainly, or they're just noise. The Lord has always been clear about what matters. So should we.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A war trumpet that sounds uncertain sends soldiers into chaos. In Corinth as it is now: clarity calls forth readiness. When God's voice comes to us, it's never fuzzy. When we speak for Him, we have a duty to be plainspoken, so the truth can land and move the heart to act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Speaking words nobody understands is like shouting into thin air. You're alone. For forty years I've watched misunderstanding tear at friendships and families—so much of it because someone spoke without caring if the other person could hear. The Lord wants His word to land in the ear and the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every sound in creation carries meaning—birds, wind, a baby's cry. Nothing the Lord made is empty noise. That truth should humble us when we speak, whether in prayer or to our neighbor. Our words, too, are weighted. They land somewhere. They mean something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If I don't understand your language, we're foreigners to each other—cut off, unable to meet. Paul's point is tender: don't leave your brothers and sisters out of the room. Don't make the church feel like babel, where people stand next to each other but can't touch. We're called to one table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You want spiritual gifts? Good—that hunger is from the Lord. But here's the test: are they building up the whole assembly, or just you? I've seen people with real power in prayer ask God to make them builders instead of stars. That's maturity. That's the fear of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you speak in a language without interpretation, you've left people behind. Paul's remedy: ask the Lord for the gift to interpret. Don't just shut up—ask for the second half. Don't let a gift sit locked up when the Spirit could unlock it for the whole room to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prayer in a tongue the Spirit alone knows—that can flow without understanding. But here's what haunts Paul: my mind is left out, unfruitful. There's a season for prayer beyond words, yes. But we're made to think too, to wrestle with truth. The Lord wants all of us awake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul offers the both-and: I'll pray with my spirit, and also with my mind. I'll sing in the Spirit, and also sing words I understand. Don't choose one lane. The deepest prayer uses everything the Lord gave you—heart, soul, mind, strength, all awake and turned toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Imagine standing in the back—the unlearned visitor—hearing someone bless God in a language you don't know. Can you even say 'Amen'? That word is your voice meeting God's, your heart joining the prayer. If you can't follow, you're locked out. Paul is saying: be merciful to those finding their way in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You might be giving thanks beautifully in a tongue nobody else speaks—and yet the person beside you feels nothing, learns nothing, leaves untouched. Paul is patient here, but firm: your joy doesn't build them. The room is not richer because you are thankful alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul himself speaks in tongues more than all of Corinth. He's not disparaging the gift—he's just showing he has the authority to say: I know this gift, I use it, and I'm telling you it's not the pinnacle. The Lord is bigger than any one thing we can do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five words with your mind intact, so others can learn—better than ten thousand words in a language they can't follow. This is Paul at his most practical. In the assembly, be the elder who speaks less but clearly. Let wisdom, not volume, fill the room.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't be children in your thinking, yet be babies in your malice. I've watched people chase experience without understanding, and I've watched others so guarded they forgot wonder. Paul is calling for maturity: think clearly about what the Lord is doing, but stay soft-hearted and free from spite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Isaiah—the Lord will speak to Israel through strangers' lips and a foreign tongue. The sign has always been there: when people hear a language they don't recognize, it gets their attention. But even then, Paul notes, they didn't hear. A sign only works if the heart is ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Speaking in a tongue is for those outside the faith—a sign that arrests them, makes them stop and wonder. Prophecy is for believers—it speaks to hearts already turning toward the Lord. Each gift has its season, its people. Use wisdom about when and where to unfold them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Picture it: the whole room speaking in languages nobody shares. A stranger walks in, hears only sound without sense, and thinks you've all lost your minds. It's the opposite of witness. The Lord came to be understood. When we gather, clarity opens the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now picture the room full of prophecy—God's truth spoken plainly. That same stranger or doubter comes in and is reproved by all. Not harshly, but the Spirit in the room touches the secrets of his heart. Truth has a voice that unbeliever can't hide from.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His hidden things are laid bare—not to shame him, but to show him that the God he didn't believe in knows him anyway. He falls on his face and worships. I've never forgotten the power of that moment—when someone realizes they're truly seen, and that seeing is love, not judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you come together, each one brings something—a psalm, teaching, revelation, a word in another language, an interpretation. It's not a stage; it's a potluck of the Spirit. But the rule is simple: let it all build each other up. No gift is meant to float alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If someone speaks in a language without a shared tongue, limit it: two or three speakers, taking turns, each with an interpreter ready. Paul is giving permission—do it—but with guardrails. The Lord loves order. It steadies the room and honors the people listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If no one can interpret, keep quiet in the assembly. But don't swallow your gift—speak to yourself and to God in private. Sometimes the answer is not 'never' but 'later' or 'elsewhere.' The Spirit speaks in the car on the way home too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophets speak, two or three, and the others discern. This is beautiful: no one prophet has a monopoly. Others listen, test what they hear against Scripture and the Spirit's whisper. Corporate discernment—the body checking itself. I've watched this keep churches from going off the rails.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If a revelation comes to someone seated nearby, the first prophet stops and sits down. Even mid-speech. There's a humility here—the Lord is not on anyone's exclusive timeline. When the Spirit moves, we step back and listen. That takes a quiet heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You can all prophesy, one at a time, so that everyone learns and everyone is encouraged. Paul trusts the assembly—not just the pastors, not just the gifted few, but each one the Lord is working through. In the long years, I've seen the deepest healing come from an ordinary voice speaking a timely word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. You are not controlled by the Spirit in a way that takes your will. The Lord doesn't override you. He persuades, prompts, guides—but you choose to speak or stay silent. That's how He honors us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God is not the God of confusion but of peace. In all the churches everywhere, the same Lord brings harmony out of many voices. When a room feels chaotic, Paul is saying, stop and ask: Is this the Spirit? The Lord's fingerprint is always peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Women are to be quiet in the assemblies, not speaking, but in submission as the law says. This verse sits hard with modern ears, and I won't pretend otherwise. Paul invokes the law—the ancient pattern. I read this alongside Priscilla teaching Apollos, and Deborah leading Israel. The Lord's truth is deeper than any one command.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If they want to learn, let them ask their own husbands at home—not in public. It was shameful in that culture for a woman to speak in the assembly. Paul gives the reason: submission. Yet he also writes elsewhere that in Christ there is neither male nor female. I hold both truths and trust the Lord knew what He was doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Did the word of God originate with you? Did it come to you alone? Paul pushes back against Corinth's pride. They thought they had special wisdom, special standing. He reminds them: you're not the first church, not the only one. Stay humble. The Lord's word is bigger than your experience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you think you're a prophet or have the Spirit's gifting, recognize what Paul writes as a command from the Lord. That's the test—submission to the apostles' teaching, to what Christ gave us. A gift proves itself by bowing to Jesus' word, not by standing apart from it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant. It's a hard mercy. Paul has reasoned, explained, shown the way. If someone won't hear, won't submit to the Lord's word—well, Paul steps back. Sometimes the kindest thing is to stop arguing and let someone live with their choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Desire earnestly to prophesy, and don't forbid speaking in other languages. Paul doesn't close the door on the second gift—he just reorders the room. Prophecy is primary because it builds the gathering. But the other gift? Let it flow, just not at the cost of what the Lord is doing in plain sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let all things be done decently and in order. Readers today hear an echo in this—the Lord cares not just about our passion but how we show up, how we hold space for each other, how the room feels to a stranger or a child. Looking back from here, I see how much healing comes from a church that's both on fire and tended with care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
